newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Tatas keen to take off in comeback airline.
newsitem.headline: India's Tatas keen to take off in comeback airline.

text.p: The Tata group, which pioneered India's aviation industry before its nationalisation, says it is hoping to stage a comeback with its proposed airline involving Singapore Airlines.

Breaking their silence on the $600 million proposal that has divided India's cabinet, Tata officials on Wednesday countered criticism from some aviation experts that their airline would hurt state-run Indian Airlines or Air-India.
"We have the highest regard for Air India. After all, we started it," Tata Industries' director Sujit Gupta told a news conference in New Delhi.
"We do not see ourselves as a threat to Indian Airlines," Gupta said in response to a question.
The Tatas are India's largest corporate group with sales in excess of 265 billion rupees ($7.5 billion) in 1995/96 (April-March).
The group owned India's main airline before independence from British rule in 1947, but the government launched a state monopoly of the skies in 1953.
Private airlines were revived after India started economic reforms in 1991.
The Tata proposal, presented in 1995, has become a test case for foreign investors.

Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim has publicly opposed the proposal to set up Tata Airlines, in which Singapore Airlines and the Tatas would hold 40 percent each, with the rest of the shareholding sold to Indian institutional investors.
Ibrahim has locked horns with Industry Minister Murasoli Maran, who supported the Tata proposal.
Last month, India approved an aviation policy that allowed foreign investors to hold stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines, but did not allow foreign airlines to directly hold any stake.
Ibrahim has said New Delhi could not allow Singapore Airlines to take a stake in an Indian airline because Singapore does not allow foreign stakes of over five percent in its domestic airlines.
But the doors are not yet closed for the Tatas. Officials say the government is yet to take a final view.
Speaking on the project's prospects, Industry Minister Maran told Reuters in an interview on Thursday: "I don't know. It has been deferred. That is all I can say."

Asked if differences within the Indian cabinet sent wrong signals to foreign investors, he said: "Differences of opinion are bound to be there in a democratic society, more so in a United Front goverment with a 13-party alliance."
Tata officials said group chairman Ratan Tata had a "good meeting" with Ibrahim last week. "We have always remained optimistic. We have waited for two years," Gupta said.

In Bombay, Ratan Tata refused to comment when buttonholed by reporters at a news conference on Thursday at the launch of another Tata company. "I made up my mind not to answer questions on this subject today," Tata said.
Tata officials said their airline would be controlled by Indians but tap Singapore Airlines' expertise in safety, managerial efficiency, service standards and training.
The Tatas said they planned to fly only 19 aircraft by 2002, while India estimated it would need 107 aircraft including 78 new planes and 29 replacements by that time.
In comparison with Indian Airlines, which already had 57 aircraft, Tata Airline would be a small player, they said.
The Tatas cited examples of domestic airlines elsewhere in the world that allow foreign airlines to hold stakes.

They said their airline would comply with Indian policy requirements which insist that domestic airlines must fly on some routes that are not financially attractive in order to provide broadbased customer service.
